title: The right model at the right moment: Vendors push their agentic AI PC vision
summary: AI is getting expensive, and companies are looking to cut token costs. The solution: move more AI work to PCs. The PC won’t replace the cloud. Preliminary AI work can be done on a PC, and tougher work — which today’s PCs can’t handle — can go to the cloud. “We’ll always need to use the most advanced cloud-based frontier models for certain tasks, but… we don’t need to use them for everything,” wrote TECHnalysis Research Insights president Bob O’Donnell in a LinkedIn post . That’s the vision Microsoft calls “hybrid intelligence,” in which Windows makes AI always available . The cloud models run the hardest tasks, and less demanding tasks run locally on the PC. For Windows machines, at least at this point, that means Copilot+ AI PCs. “The future of AI is not about having just one model. It’s about having the right model at the right moment — frontier capability when you need it, smaller, faster models when you want speed,” said Pavan Davuluri, head of Windows and Devices at Microsoft, at an Oct. 7 PC launch event. Hybrid intelligence will be everywhere, blurring the line between AI in the cloud and the PC, said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella at the event. “I just want to use my computing power wherever it is in sort of a seamless flow of what I’m trying to get done,” he said. Agentic AI PCs Microsoft recognizes that hefty cloud token bills are making enterprises hesitate to scale AI. Its answer: offload AI tasks that don’t need cloud models to AI PCs. About 10% to 15% of AI workloads will run on PCs and 40% to 45% in the cloud in the next three to four years, said analyst Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates. “Companies will need AI-accelerated PCs, and at some point we’ll likely see a renewed emphasis on buying newer machines,” Gold said. Enter agentic AI PCs , which can run agents, generate video, write code and chat with advanced genAI models on a PC. If the PC can’t do the job, it is sent to the cloud. “A year ago, such capabilities were exclusive to frontier cloud models.

title: Apple confirms iPhone Duo problem. What will it do next?

What Apple will do now I imagine that what is happening now is that Apple is gathering intelligence as damaged units are returned to AppleCare. Speculatively, the cause could be something as simple as a misaligned tool on the production line, though the fact that the problem doesn’t impact every iPhone Duo suggests it is not necessarily inherent to the design of the product. If I’m right and Apple has identified the problem as a manufacturing issue, then Apple representatives will be in crisis contact with their suppliers to track the problem down and resolve it. That’s going to mean a little lost production while factory production lines are checked and verified, and whatever problem is causing these faults is hopefully resolved. title: No signal, no problem: Smaller models bring more AI capabilities on-device
summary: When OpenAI’s GPT-3 was released in 2020, at 175 billion parameters, it was the largest language model the world had ever seen. In the years that followed, frontier AI systems exploded in size, with today’s largest models clocking in at well over a trillion parameters. But there is a countercurrent of AI research moving in the opposite direction, with pioneers like Tether building a new generation of smaller AI models . Requiring a fraction of the computing power of their heavyweight cousins, this emerging field of lightweight models is driving a shift toward more on-device AI, with a growing range of applications now able to run locally, rather than relying on the cloud. At around four billion parameters, even the largest among Tether’s suite of compact models is tiny compared to frontier AI systems, while others are small enough to run on a basic smartphone, without requiring an internet connection once downloaded. Mega models and the limits of scaling As AI labs have pursued larger context windows, more sophisticated reasoning, and multimodal capabilities, model sizes have increased significantly in recent years, to the extent that parameter count, cluster size, and megawatt consumption are often framed as proxies for performance. This narrative assumes that bigger is always better, and for a while, it was. Research has demonstrated the existence of scaling laws: predictable mathematical relationships showing that increasing model parameters, training data, and compute power led directly to superior performance and emergent capabilities. To build more intelligent systems, frontier AI developers simply had to throw more resources at the challenge. The problem is that brute force AI scaling offers diminishing returns. And while global data center capacity is expanding rapidly, the supply of human-generated training data that fueled language model growth until now is increasingly depleted . title: Elon Musk says he has ‘cyber psychosis’. Do you too? | Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Whether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signs In the least surprising news you’ll hear all week, Elon Musk has said he’s not entirely right in the head. “I’ve got a little bit of cyber psychosis,” the world’s richest and most irritating man explained during an event this month. “Maybe a lot actually.” Musk added that, over “various points this year”, he’s had “AI or SI psychosis probably half a dozen times”. SI, in case you missed the super-important memo, stands for “ superintelligence ” and it’s what Donald Trump wants everyone to call AI now, for reasons too stupid to explain. While the phrase SI is still being used 0nly by weaselly tech bros desperate for Trump’s approval, you’ll probably have heard the term “ AI psychosis ” bandied around a lot. On the most serious level, it refers to delusional thinking induced or exacerbated by sycophantic chatbots. People who have ploughed their life savings into a ridiculous business idea, for example, because computer code told them they were the next Jeff Bezos. But the phrase has also been used more jokingly to describe overexuberance around artificial intelligence, and that seems to be how Musk was using it. The comments about his self-diagnosed bouts of cyber psychosis came as the tech mogul waxed lyrical about how great AI music videos have become, and how he believes artificial intelligence now “understands beauty and harmony”. title: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic
summary: It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t Think back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and without having seen the film, condemned the supposed wokery in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, for getting Elliot Page to play Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen of Troy? As the plaudits and the box-office receipts for Nolan’s Odyssey piled stratospherically up , Musk showed that being a good loser is not among his qualities. He petulantly exclaimed that he could do his own better and more authentic Odyssey on Grok AI . And now he has released the first online seven-minute “episode” to a world that has long since forgotten about this claim and didn’t care in the first place. In Musk’s version, as the tale begins Odysseus is – off screen – pretending to be mad to avoid fighting in the Trojan war. Grim-faced Palamedes and Agamemnon are shown testing this ruse by taking his baby boy Telemachus and placing him in the harm’s way of a plough in a field; Odysseus instantly rushes to save his child, showing that he isn’t mad, and agrees to fight. We see him join the armada, with Penelope and Telemachus (soon to grow to a little boy) left behind. This, effectively, is a prologue sequence that is not in Nolan. The expeditionary force arrives at Troy, and an intertitle tells us we have cut to a 10-years-later flashforward; the siege is about to escalate into the fake-horse attack. Continue reading...

title: Python jettisons the native JIT, at least for now
summary: The experimental just-in-time compiler, or JIT, for CPython will be removed after its maintainers missed deadlines for its formalization set by the Python Steering Council. According to reporting at LWN.net , the move comes after the council formally paused work on the JIT in June 2026 until it approved a Python Enhancement Proposal, or PEP, that described how the JIT could become a properly supported part of CPython. The JIT’s proponents, Brandt Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski, originally drafted PEP 744 to explain the JIT’s functionality, but this document did not explain how the JIT would be maintained and integrated in CPython. To answer that, they offered PEP 836 , but still ran into pushback from the council, which found that PEP 836 lacked sufficient details about how the JIT would be supported, its performance would be evaluated, and how it would be integrated with debugging and profiling tools. The council also criticized the PEP for being overly optimistic about the performance gains to expect. Speed improvements for the CPython JIT were measurable, but small, and only improved performance for some classes of programs, such as those with long-running tight loops. On October 19, PEP 836 was withdrawn. “The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don’t feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward,” Ostrowski said. “We continue to believe in the technical direction outlined in the PEP, including free-threaded support and a method-based front end, and remain optimistic about the JIT’s potential in CPython.” Nothing forbids other developers from continuing where the JIT project left off. Withdrawing PEP 836 simply means that work on the JIT in the mainline edition of CPython won’t go forward. Other developers are free to continue the work in their own way, perhaps in an alternative build of CPython, although they will face the same high bar if they want to contribute that work back to CPython. title: Digital sovereignty as a design requirement
summary: Digital sovereignty has moved from a policy discussion to a practical enterprise cloud computing problem. For years, most organizations treated public cloud as a location-flexible utility. They placed workloads where performance, price, managed services, and availability looked best. Data residency requirements existed, of course, but they were often handled as narrow legal or compliance tasks. Pick the right region, write the right contract language, encrypt the data, and move on. That approach is no longer enough. Enterprises now operate in a world where governments, regulators, customers, and boards are asking hard questions about who controls data, who can access systems, where operational authority resides, and what happens when geopolitical, legal, or provider-level risks collide with cloud architectures. Digital sovereignty is not simply about where data sits. It is about who has effective control over the data, the infrastructure, the encryption keys, the operations, the administrators, the support model, and the legal jurisdiction around the entire cloud stack. Sovereignty is now a much larger issue than most cloud teams expected. Sovereignty is becoming broader The earliest version of digital sovereignty was mostly about data residency. Could an enterprise guarantee that customer records, financial data, health data, or government information remained within a specific country or region? Public cloud providers responded with more regions, more availability zones, and more contractual assurances. That helped, but it did not solve the full problem. Modern sovereignty discussions include data residency, operational control, legal exposure, software supply chains, administrative access, encryption key ownership, dependency on foreign providers, and the ability to continue operating if political or regulatory conditions change. Enterprises need to understand that a workload can satisfy a basic data residency requirement and still fail a broader sovereignty test

title: Robot eyeballs make open source more valuable
summary: “Bug-free, secure code is now attainable” is a nice idea . It just happens to be wrong. That ambitious statement was one of more than 80 replies to Eric Raymond’s optimistic take on AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries. Because the corpus of human-written code is finite, Raymond argues, so are its defects. With “a million friendly robots” to help fix them, we’re well-positioned to out-AI the bad guys and secure our software. I’m all for that. The problem is treating this as a bug hunt we’re going to finish. Today’s tools are uncovering holes in yesterday’s code. Why assume tomorrow’s tools won’t do the same to software we consider secure today? For those of us who have spent decades arguing for open source, this is an interesting development. Raymond popularized Linus’s law: “Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.” Making source available never guaranteed enough qualified eyeballs, and let’s be real, few people ever cared to look. AI is finally putting more of those eyeballs to work. They just happen to be robots. The open source opportunity lies in what we choose to do next. I strongly believe we need open source today more than ever: A shared codebase gives successive generations of bug hunters somewhere to contribute fixes everyone can use. It’s also, as I recently argued in my All Things Open keynote, a way for us to collectively decide which software matters and why. When generating another codebase becomes easy, that choice matters more. The bug hunt doesn’t end As I’ve written , open source code was never inherently more secure. Few people inspected it. The strength was that when someone found a problem, the code and the process were open enough to do something about it. AI makes the discovery part more interesting. In November 2024, Google reported 26 vulnerabilities found using AI-generated fuzz targets in projects that had already undergone hundreds of thousands of hours of fuzzing. title: When GraphQL earns its place in an enterprise application, and when it doesn’t

In all other cases, there is a price to pay, which is bound to come out after you have already made the decision. I build internal access-governance applications, with React front ends that talk to both REST and GraphQL back ends. Using the two side by side has shown me where each earns its keep and where each gets in the way. The article is divided into three sections. The first section covers areas in which GraphQL eliminates round trips and front-end work. The second section highlights the underestimated costs involved. Finally, there are a few questions you can ask yourself before implementing the GraphQL approach. GraphQL helps most on screens built from connected data Imagine the details screen for one client. On this screen, you see the client, his/her accounts, permissions for these accounts, owners of these accounts and some related objects for each. Data is highly interrelated, and your screen requires some portion of each layer at once. There are two scenarios for working with REST API. In the first scenario, the front end makes several requests – first for the client, then for his accounts and then for permissions of each of those accounts. Each request in the chain waits for the preceding request to be finished. Another scenario is when the back end creates a specific endpoint in the desired format. The first one becomes very inefficient whenever the network has some issues. The second one works well as long as the information that is to appear on the next screen appears in the same format as before, but then you get many endpoints nobody cares about maintaining. With the help of GraphQL, it becomes possible to change the decision-maker of the shape. The client asks for the query with the specific fields and receives the response in the specific format. A neat feature of the badge is that you can turn it upside down and then use game controller touch buttons that are built into the badge body. title: Landed a new job - thank you /r/DE
summary: Title. Recently landed a new DE gig after searching casually for the majority of this year. I applied for about 30 jobs over the course of 2026. I was at a dead end with my old place, dealing with a ton of micromanagement and a botched migration from SSIS to ADF that left everything more complicated than it was when it was on-prem and no hope of migrating off of it. Old company tech stack: SQL Server, SSIS, ADF(Azure), Snowflake. Pretty repetitive from an engineering point of view. New gig came with a 30% pay bump, no on-call, and better benefits. The tech stack is mostly legacy stuff, but they're hiring for an architect and staffing up up the DE team (which is why I got the job) because they're trying to modernize everything. I got the job because I have experience with older on-prem stuff and some newer cloud stuff. New company is a highly-regulated industry (power), so things are pretty slow moving in the IT area, hence all the legacy stuff still in place. New company tech stack: Talend, Snowflake, Azure, Exadata, Denodo, Informatica Catalog, Monte Carlo. They already have a lot running in Snowflake, and the endgame goal is to get more moved up there over the next few years. I've got a couple weeks off before I start at the new gig so I'm gonna take on a homelab project or 3 this weekend. Just wanted to say thank you to the /r/DE community for being a soundboard for me a few times this year, and hopefully provide some inspiration for folks out there who feel like the market is all doom and gloom. In the interviews that I had for the job I landed, I focused a bit more on the migration efforts that I've been a part of and focused on the business intel side of things, not simply the code and tools. Yes, the market is tough and over-saturated right now, I don't want to dismiss that - but the reality is that companies still need engineers, and businesses still need business intelligence, so there will still be jobs out there. Cheers! submitted by /u/lostmyway573 [link
